Arab-Islamic historians describe this intermediary role in their own way when they discuss the famous winter and summer trading journeys mentioned in the Qur’an, Surah Quraysh 106. Their accounts give us a picture of the relations between the leaders of Quraysh—Hashim ibn Abd Manaf, Abd Shams, al-Muttalib ibn Abd Manaf, and Nawfal ibn Abd Manaf—and the rulers of Iraq, Syria, and Ethiopia. They describe agreements resembling commercial treaties that guaranteed protection for trading caravans serving the interests of those rulers. See al-Ya‘qubi, History, vol. 2, p. 282; al-Baladhuri, Genealogies of the Nobles, ed. Muhammad Hamidullah, 1959, vol. 1, p. 59; and al-Qalqashandi, Subh al-A‘sha, vol. 1, p. 358.↩︎

Harrat is the plural of harra. As Yaqut defines it in Dictionary of Countries, quoting Kitab al-Ayn, it is “land covered with black, porous stones as though they had been burned by fire.” In other words, these are remains of ancient volcanic activity. Such lava fields are scattered between eastern Hawran and Medina, or Yathrib. Yaqut lists twenty-nine of them. One is Harra Waqim, where the Battle of al-Harra took place during the caliphate of Yazid ibn Mu‘awiya in 63 AH. See Dictionary of Countries, vol. 2, pp. 245–246.↩︎

Reports from the late pre-Islamic period show that agricultural regions, especially Yathrib and Ta’if, processed some fruits and plants in ways that amounted to small-scale production. This included making wine from dates, drying fruit, making containers to preserve and transport it over long distances, and extracting timber from tamarisk and athl trees for carpentry. See Salim, p. 405. They also seem to have known how to make dyes for coloring fabrics, since they cultivated plants used in producing dye materials. See Belyaev, p. 92.↩︎

The Arabian Peninsula was not fully surveyed geographically until the period between the First and Second World Wars. Even in the mid-nineteenth century, Europeans knew no more about the vast interior of the peninsula than they knew about the visible surface of the moon. Belyaev, p. 55. That concerns physical geography, which remains stable over very long periods. Economic and human geography, by contrast, changes and develops. It is still the obscure—if not missing—link in the history of the pre-Islamic period.↩︎

A report says that one of the polishers polished the Prophet’s sword Dhu al-Fiqar. Its pommel—the piece at the end of the handle—its rings in the strap, and a central fitting were made of silver. See al-Baladhuri, Genealogies of the Nobles, p. 521. This shows a form of metalworking that had reached a considerable level of technical skill.↩︎

Engels regards the human use of iron for tools and implements as one feature of the stage from which society passes into civilization after the discovery of alphabetic writing. See Engels, The Origin of the Family, Arabic ed., p. 42. Historians agree that the pre-Islamic Arabs knew alphabetic writing, as we will see shortly.↩︎

al-Baladhuri says in Genealogies of the Nobles that Amr, son of al-As ibn Wa’il al-Sahmi, said of his father that he used to ride a donkey to his estate in Ta’if, vol. 1, p. 139. He also reports, p. 57, that Abu Talib, the Prophet’s uncle, received raisins from a vineyard he owned in Ta’if. All of this shows that productive land ownership in Ta’if by leaders of Quraysh was commonplace.↩︎

In a specialized study of Ethiopian slaves in the Hijaz, Lammens says that leading members of Quraysh from the Meccan mala’ armed these slaves and used them to guard their homes, commercial caravans, and the Ka‘ba, which served as a storehouse for their wealth. It is useful to quote Jawad Ali here. He writes: “Captives—that is, prisoners—were a thriving trade in those days, bringing enormous profits and great wealth to those who practiced it. The peninsula was one of the most important markets importing this merchandise in all colors—white, black, and shades in between—and of both sexes. The two great states, Rome and Persia, sold whatever prisoners of war they did not need from the defeated side in the markets, or sent this expensive merchandise through brokers to the markets of the peninsula for sale there. They might also give thousands of captives to tribal shaykhs in order to win their favor, and these shaykhs would then sell the gift to willing buyers.” History of the Arabs before Islam, vol. 4, p. 165. Arab chroniclers provide many reports about Qurayshi leaders involved in the slave trade, such as Abdallah ibn Jud‘an and others. See, for example, al-Baladhuri, Genealogies, vol. 1, p. 467 ff.↩︎

The ordinary ransom for each captive was one hundred camels. But this could rise depending on the prisoner’s standing among his people or his wealth. In the battle known as the Day of al-Sallan, Wabra al-Kalbi was ransomed for one thousand camels and a horse. See Yaqut, Dictionary of Countries, vol. 5, p. 104.↩︎

The words dirham and dinar both appear in the Qur’an: “They sold him for a small price, a few dirhams, and cared little for him” (Qur’an 12:20); and “Among the People of the Book are some who, if you entrust them with a great treasure, will return it to you, while others, if you entrust them with a single dinar, will not return it unless you keep demanding it” (Qur’an 3:75).↩︎

Belyaev, p. 136. Jawad Ali, vol. 8, p. 200 ff., says that examples have been found of local coins used by the people of southern Arabia in their transactions. Some were struck in gold, some in silver, others in copper and other metals. Museums, antiquities collections, and private collections contain coins struck in southern Arabia, some in gold, some in silver, and others in copper. Some small coins carry the name of the king during whose reign they were struck. Some, however, are ancient and go back to the period before the Common Era. Jawad Ali also argues, same source, p. 206, that the people of the Hijaz used not only Roman and Sasanian coins—dinars, dirhams, and daniq—but also Yemeni and Ethiopian coins in the pre-Islamic period and in early Islam before Islamic coins with Arabic inscriptions were struck. Meccans in particular traded with Yemen, Iraq, and Syria and therefore used many different currencies. Conditions in their own country were not favorable for minting coins locally.↩︎

al-Baladhuri reports, quoting al-Kalbi, that Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim ibn Abd Manaf offered twenty ounces of gold or ten camels as ransom for Hudhafa ibn Ghanim al-Adawi. Genealogies, vol. 1, p. 66.↩︎

One revealing example shows that private ownership of livestock was widespread. al-Aghani, vol. 16, p. 95, tells a story about Hatim al-Ta’i, who died forty-five years before the Hijra. Banu Lam wanted to compete with Hatim at the market of al-Hira by making a wager involving his horse. When Iyas ibn Qabisa al-Ta’i heard of this, he feared Hatim might be defeated and lose the wager, so he gathered his people from Banu Hayya and urged them to support their cousin Hatim. One man said: “I have one hundred black camels and one hundred reddish camels.” Another stood and said: “I have ten stallions, each with a fully armed rider.” Hassan ibn Jabala al-Khayr said: “You know that my father died and left great wealth. I will provide all the wine, meat, and food for as long as they remain at the market of al-Hira.” Iyas then said: “I will give as much as all of you together.” The story continues that Hatim’s cousin Wahm ibn Amr said: “No. This is my property, numbering nine hundred camels. Take it from him until the camels are exhausted or you get what you want.” The story also appears in Stories of the Arabs, by Muhammad Ahmad Jad al-Mawla and his colleagues, Cairo, 1948, vol. 3, pp. 98–99. Hatim’s own verse is significant here: “They say to me: You have wasted your wealth, so be moderate / Yet without the very things they criticize, I would never have been a chief.”↩︎

Two concrete examples illustrate this kind of ownership. 1. It is said that during the reign of King al-Nu‘man (583–605), Hajib ibn Zurara and Qays ibn Mas‘ud argued over which man among their peoples was the meanest. Al-Nu‘man sent someone to see and testify. When they reached the territory of Hajib ibn Zurara, they passed a man from his people, and Hajib said: “This is the meanest of my people.” The man was beside his water basin, watering his camels. See Mahmud Shukri al-Alusi, Reaching the Goal, Cairo, 1923, vol. 1, p. 286. Note the phrase “his basin”: the water source was therefore this man’s property. The rest of the story says that he refused to give these people water from “his basin” even after learning that their tribal chief Hajib ibn Zurara was among them, although the story says that they had “entered Hajib’s territory.” 2. In a story about Qays ibn al-Khatim, who died in 2 AH, when he set out to avenge the killers of his father and grandfather, he went to his water-drawing camel while it was irrigating his palm grove. A nadih is the camel used to turn the waterwheel. See al-Aghani, vol. 3, p. 3. Here Qays ibn al-Khatim clearly owns a garden, along with a well or irrigation channel from which he waters it using his own waterwheel driven by his camel.↩︎
